claim.quote: I don't really crown something a winner just because it drives the most of your sales.

units.title: New $30/day account test with 13 ads and 800 impression limit

claim.text: In a new account spending $30 a day, the source launched 13 ads, initially set an impression limit of 1,000, saw CPMs around $50-$70, and lowered the limit to 800 to finish efficiently without blowing the budget.
claim.quote: we started working with a new account spending $30 a day, and I'm going to show you our exact creative test. In here, you can see that we launched 13 ads. They're spending $30 a day, so we don't have really that much budget here. I initially set our impression limit to 1,000, just so we can get done with this test pretty quickly. But, I noticed that our CPMs were on average like 50, 60, 70 dollars. And so, that means, and I I saw the comments from the other video, you know, $17 CPA is really unrealistic. This is a little bit more realistic with a newer account with a pixel that doesn't have much data to lower our CPM. And so, with that, we had to lower our impression limit to 800 just to make sure that we finish this test efficiently without blowing through a ton of budget.

unknowns: The source says CPMs were on average like $50, $60, $70 but does not give a precise average.

units.title: Use the stairway approach: identify, test, win, move up

claim.quote: You identify the variable, test it, find a winner, and then move up to the next variable and leaving behind everything weighing you down even if it's a little bit, even if it's 5 cent cost per [music] click. And testing creative should work the exact same way.

units.title: Read creative performance through the customer journey

claim.text: When reading why a creative won or lost, the source says to think about the customer journey: first attention, then click to site, then post-click data.
claim.quote: when you read why the creative won or lost, you have to think about the customer journey like how we saw here. First, did we get their attention? If nobody stops, maybe the hook isn't strong enough. Maybe the visual itself just isn't that interesting. Then we ask, did they click to the site? If people are watching and nobody's clicking, well, maybe the creative is entertaining but the product and the value isn't compelling or even being communicated. Maybe they don't understand why they need this product.

input.text: re [music] we get into the actual creative testing because let's say I like this angle. Get your steps in while you work without needing a giant treadmill. I don't want to necessarily abandon that idea and make 10 completely different ads. I might make two versions here. Version one, maybe that's a UGC video. Version two could be a carousel where the slides tell the story. General same angle, the same product, same argument, different opening. Now, if one massively outperforms the others, we've actually learned something. And I know video and carousel, you know, there may be a very big difference, but you use this in your own scenarios here. And when you do find something, then we can discuss what's the best kind of ad to make next. And all of this is a big part of how we approach paid media [music] at ADVT.
